pool.prompt: A fiber link has: Tx = +5 dBm, Rx sensitivity = -22 dBm, fiber = 25 km x 0.25 dB/km, 8 splices x 0.15 dB, 6 connectors x 0.30 dB, 3 dB safety margin. Does this link pass?
choices: Yes — headroom is positive
No — headroom is negative
Yes, but just barely — headroom is 0 dB
Cannot be determined without knowing the fiber type
pool.explanation: Budget = 5 - (-22) = 27 dB. Losses: fiber = 25 x 0.25 = 6.25 dB, splices = 8 x 0.15 = 1.20 dB, connectors = 6 x 0.30 = 1.80 dB, margin = 3.00 dB. Total = 12.25 dB. Headroom = 27.0 - 12.25 = 14.75 dB. Link passes with 14.75 dB headroom.

pool.prompt: Why does a link budget always include a 'safety margin' (typically 3 dB) that is reserved and never allocated to components?
choices: To account for the loss introduced by the OTDR measurement cable
To reserve optical power for fiber aging, thermal effects, connector wear over time, and future re-splices
Because TIA-568 requires a 3 dB mandatory reserve on all SMF links
To account for the difference between 1310 nm and 1550 nm planning values
pool.explanation: Optical fiber plant degrades over time: fiber attenuation increases slightly with age and temperature cycling; connectors accumulate contamination and wear; splice cases experience freeze-thaw stress. A 3 dB margin ensures the link still works after decades of service, re-splices, and component replacements.
pool.fieldNote: On RUS-financed projects with 30+ year design life expectations, a 3 dB safety margin is standard practice; some customers require 4-5 dB. Removing it to squeeze in more distance is a deferred failure.

pool.prompt: If Tx power = +3 dBm and Rx sensitivity = -25 dBm, what is the available optical budget?
choices: 22 dB
28 dB
-22 dB
3 dB

pool.prompt: A link budget totals 27 dB available and 20 dB of accumulated component + fiber loss (before margin). If the designer requires a 3 dB safety margin, what is the actual remaining headroom after reserving the margin?
choices: 7 dB
4 dB
10 dB
0 dB — the margin consumes all remaining headroom
pool.explanation: 27 dB budget - 20 dB accumulated loss - 3 dB reserved margin = 4 dB remaining headroom. The margin is subtracted as its own line item alongside fiber, splice, and connector losses, not left as an afterthought.

pool.prompt: What four categories of loss (or reserve) typically appear as line items in an OSP fiber link budget calculation?
choices: Fiber attenuation, splice loss, connector loss, and safety margin
Only fiber attenuation and splice loss — connectors and margin are not part of a formal budget
Tx power, Rx power, ambient temperature, and cable color
PMD, chromatic dispersion, and two redundant margin allowances
pool.explanation: A standard link budget worksheet totals: fiber attenuation (length x dB/km), splice loss (count x per-splice loss), connector loss (count x per-connector loss), and a reserved safety margin — subtracted from the Tx-Rx power budget to determine pass/fail headroom.

pool.prompt: A link budget shows negative headroom after accounting for all losses and margin. What does this mean, and what are valid design responses?
choices: Nothing — negative headroom is fine as long as the fiber physically reaches the destination

The link will not reliably operate as designed; valid responses include reducing splice/connector count, choosing a lower-loss wavelength, upgrading to higher-power optics, or reducing/re-evaluating the safety margin only with strong justification
Negative headroom only matters for MMF links, not SMF
The designer should ignore it since real fiber always performs better than calculated
pool.explanation: Negative headroom means the design, as specified, will not reliably deliver enough signal to the receiver. The correct response is redesign — not proceeding and hoping real-world performance beats the worst-case calculation, since the whole point of the budget is to avoid exactly that gamble.

pool.prompt: In the worked example (Tx=+5dBm, Rx=-22dBm, 25km fiber @0.25dB/km, 8 splices @0.15dB, 6 connectors @0.30dB, 3dB margin), what is the single largest individual contributor to total loss?
choices: The connectors (1.80 dB total)
The fiber attenuation (6.25 dB total)
The splices (1.20 dB total)
The safety margin (3.00 dB total)
pool.explanation: Fiber attenuation (25 km x 0.25 dB/km = 6.25 dB) is the largest single contributor in this example — larger than splices, connectors, or the margin individually. On longer links, fiber attenuation typically dominates the loss budget.

pool.prompt: Why might a customer require a larger safety margin (4-5 dB) than the standard 3 dB on some projects?
choices: Larger margins are always mandatory under FCC rules
The customer may want extra tolerance for anticipated future splice additions, harsher environmental conditions, or a longer-than-standard design life expectation beyond what a 3 dB margin covers
A larger margin means the fiber physically travels farther
Margin size has no relationship to design life or future maintenance
pool.explanation: The safety margin exists to absorb future degradation and modification. A customer anticipating more aggressive future splicing, harsher climate exposure, or an extended design-life requirement may reasonably specify a larger reserve than the 3 dB baseline.
